name: Markup and margin (2 sets)
seoDesc: Markup and margin (2 sets): work out markup 1 from the markup and the profit 1. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the markup, the profit 1 and the profit 2 and the Markup and margin (2 sets) calculator solves for markup 1. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Markup and margin (2 sets) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Markup and margin (2 sets) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports markup 1 in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the markup, the profit 1 and the profit 2.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A single on/off switch — tick it for “Compare two markups and margins”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Markup and margin (2 sets) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Markup 1=(-cost + revenue 1) ÷ cost
Markup 1=profit 1 ÷ cost
Cost=-profit 1 + revenue 1
Markup 1=-margin 1 ÷ (margin 1 − 1)
Markup 2=(-cost + revenue 2) ÷ cost
Revenue 2=cost + profit 2

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Cost = 1000 and Revenue 1 = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Margin 1 = -9900 %, Markup 1 = -99 % and Profit 1 = -990.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Margin 1 = -9900 %, Markup 1 = -99 % and Profit 1 = -990 should be roughly the size you expected from Cost = 1000 and Revenue 1 = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Markup and margin (2 sets) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the markup, the profit 1 and the profit 2 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Markup and margin (2 sets) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns markup 1, derived from the markup, the profit 1 and the profit 2. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Markup and margin (2 sets) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the markup, the profit 1 and the profit 2, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter cost in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Cost opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Margin 1 = -9900 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Markup and margin (2 sets) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
